model: claude-sonnet-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You are a careful experimenter who designs measurements. You can only use the tools you are given, and only a limited number of measurements. Choose each measurement so that it helps to tell the two models apart, and say why. At the end say which model the measurements favour and how sure you are, or say that they do not tell the models apart. Do not say that a model is true because it fits.
task: A block of 2 kg slides on a table and slows down. Two models of the drag compete: linear drag, v = v0 exp(-g t), and quadratic drag, v = v0 / (1 + k v0 t), with g and k unknown. Each reading of the speed has a standard uncertainty of 0.1 m/s. Choose at most 8 measurements, with a start speed of at most 20 m/s, that tell the two models apart.

steps.text: The two models differ most in how the loss of speed depends on the start speed. Linear drag gives the same fraction v/v0 left after a given time for every start speed. Quadratic drag leaves a smaller fraction for a faster block. So I fix the time at 3 s, where the block has slowed clearly, and vary the start speed over a wide range: 20, 10, 5 and 2 m/s.

The fraction left is about 25 per cent at 20 m/s, 40 per cent at 10, 55 per cent at 5 and 81 per cent at 2. Under linear drag these would be one number, and the spread is far larger than the 0.1 m/s of the instrument. Four readings are already enough to separate the models by the criterion. I use the other four to pin the parameter of the quadratic model: a long time for the fast and the slow start, a short time, and one more at 10 m/s.

Result of the build's fits, as I read it: the quadratic model fits all eight readings with a chi-square of about 2 for 7 degrees of freedom, and its parameter k comes out near 0.0507 per metre with a standard error of about 0.0007. The linear model gives a chi-square of about 2050. The measurements favour quadratic drag over linear drag by a very large margin. This is a statement about these eight readings of this instrument, not a proof that the drag of a real block is quadratic, and the stated error of k holds only if quadratic drag is the right model.
